title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 1.4.1 Writing: Functional Writing

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A form is a paper or screen with labels and blank spaces where we write information. In this sub-strand you will learn which details a form asks for, how to read the instructions, and how to fill personal and school information correctly and honestly.

## Strand 1.0: The Family
Sub-strand 1.4.1: Writing: Functional Writing
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the required information to be filled in forms for different purposes
b) fill information in forms correctly for self- expression
c) realise the importance of filling forms correctly for effective communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Filling forms

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should one be careful when filling in forms?
2. What information do we fill in forms?

## Core competencies
• Creativity and Imagination: This is promoted as the learner generates ideas and uses them to create a form and shares it with peers.
• Digital Literacy: It is enhanced as the learner manipulates digital devices to download, create and fill in forms.

## Values
• Love: This is promoted as the learner accommodates other’s contributions as they work jointly to fill in forms.
• Integrity : This is promoted as the learner willingly displays their forms for peer review and feedback.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Gender Education: This is promoted as the learner interacts with content about the various people and genders in the theme of family.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of filling in forms to their learning in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 1.0 The Family, Sub-strand 1.4.1 Functional Writing

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: What information goes on a form

LESSON 1: WHAT INFORMATION GOES ON A FORM
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a form is used for.
• Name the personal details and school details a simple form asks for.
• Match each piece of information to the correct label.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the required information to be filled in forms for different purposes

## Introduction
When a learner joins a school club, the club does not guess the learner's name. It gives a form. Each blank line has a job, and the writer puts the right fact on the right line.

## Notes
### What a form is
A form is a prepared sheet, or a page on a screen, that collects the same facts from many people. Clubs, schools, clinics and libraries use forms. The title at the top tells you the purpose, for example School Club Membership Form or Visitor's Book.

A form has three kinds of writing already printed on it:

- a title, which says what the form is for
- instructions, which tell you how to fill it
- labels, which name each blank, such as Name or Grade

You do not invent new labels. You fill the blanks the form already has.

### Personal details
Personal details are facts about you.

- Name: your names in the order the form asks, often surname first, then other names
- Grade: the class you are in, such as Grade 4
- Date of birth: the day, month and year you were born
- Sometimes gender: whether you are a boy or a girl. Write the answer that is true for you.

Families include people of different genders: mothers and fathers, sisters and brothers, grandmothers and grandfathers. A form may ask about one of them, for example "Name of parent or guardian". Read the label so you write the right person.

### School details
School details are facts about your school.

- Name of school
- Address: where the school is found, such as a road, a village or a town, and a box number if the school has one
- Name of class teacher
- Name of head teacher

If you do not know a school detail, ask your teacher. Do not guess a name or an address.

### A sample, not a real pupil
Look at how the blanks match the labels. This pupil is made up for practice.

Personal details
Name: Amina Yusuf
Grade: 4
Date of birth: 14 March 2017

School details
Name: Green Valley Primary School
Address: P.O. Box 25, Hill Road
Name of class teacher: Mr Otieno
Name of head teacher: Mrs Wanjala

Every fact sits on its own line. The date uses day, then month, then year. Names begin with capital letters.

### Different forms, different facts
A library form may ask for the title of a book. A clinic card may ask for a parent's phone number. Always let the label tell you what to write. The question to ask is: what does this form need, and which of my true details answers that label?

## Key words
• form — a paper or screen with labels and spaces for information
• personal details — facts about a person, such as name and date of birth
• label — the printed words that tell you what to write in a blank
• date of birth — the day, month and year a person was born

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A form says "Name of class teacher". Amina writes her own name. What is wrong?

Working:
1. Read the label again.
2. The label asks for the teacher, not the learner.
3. Amina's name belongs on the line labelled Name under personal details.

Answer: She put her own name on the class teacher's line. That line needs the teacher's name.

### Example 2
Which section does "P.O. Box 25, Hill Road" belong to: personal details or school details?

Working:
1. A box number and place name of this kind is an address.
2. On this form the address is listed under school details.

Answer: School details, on the address line.

## Activity: Sort the details
You will need: Strips of paper with these facts: your grade, a sample date of birth, a school name, a class teacher's name, a head teacher's name, a learner's name, a school address, A large sheet divided into Personal details and School details
1. In a group, read each strip and decide whether it is a personal detail or a school detail.
2. Place it under the correct heading and say which label it matches: Name, Grade, Date of birth, School name, Address, Class teacher or Head teacher.
3. Look at the sample form in the lesson and check that every fact is under the right label.
4. Tell the group one fact a library form might ask for that this school form does not ask for.

## Practice
1. Name three personal details this lesson's form asks for.
2. Name three school details this lesson's form asks for.
3. Where should the head teacher's name be written?
4. What does the title of a form tell you?

## Summary
• A form collects the same kind of facts from many people.
• Personal details are about you. School details are about your school.
• Each fact belongs on the line whose label asks for it.

### Answers to practice
1. Name, grade and date of birth.
2. School name, address, and the name of the class teacher or the head teacher.
3. On the line labelled Name of head teacher, under school details.
4. What the form is for, or its purpose.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Reading instructions and filling a form

LESSON 2: READING INSTRUCTIONS AND FILLING A FORM
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Follow written instructions on a form.
• Fill personal and school details in the correct spaces.
• Check a filled form for missing or misplaced information.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the required information to be filled in forms for different purposes; b) fill information in forms correctly for self- expression

## Introduction
Two learners can know the same facts and still hand in different forms. The careful one reads the instructions before writing. The hurried one puts the date where the name should be.

## Notes
### Read before you write
Instructions are the sentences that tell you how to fill the form. They may say:

- Use capital letters.
- Use a pen, not a pencil.
- Write one letter or number in each box.
- Do not leave any blank empty.
- Write the date as day, month and year.

Read every instruction with a partner before anyone writes. If a word is new, ask. Guessing can put a fact in the wrong shape. For example, if the form wants 14/03/2017 and you write March 14th, you have not followed the instruction.

### How to fill each blank
1. Read the label.
2. Think of the true fact that matches it.
3. Write neatly in print, on the line, not above the label.
4. Start names with capital letters: Amina Yusuf, not amina yusuf.
5. Write Grade as a number if that is what the form shows, for example 4.
6. Write the date of birth in the order the instruction gives.

In class you may fill a practice form with your own school details. If you are not sure of the school's address or the head teacher's name, leave that blank empty until the teacher tells you. An empty blank you still need to check is better than a made-up address.

### A worked form
Instructions: Write in print. Use capital letters for names. Write the date as day, month, year.

Name: AMINA YUSUF
Grade: 4
Date of birth: 14 March 2017
School: GREEN VALLEY PRIMARY SCHOOL
Address: P.O. BOX 25, HILL ROAD
Class teacher: MR OTIENO
Head teacher: MRS WANJALA

This is still the sample pupil from the previous lesson. Notice that every instruction was kept: print, capital letters for names, and the date in day-month-year order.

### Check with a partner
Swap forms. Ask these questions:

- Is every required blank filled?
- Is each fact next to the right label?
- Are names easy to read?
- Does the date follow the instruction?
- Would a stranger understand it without asking?

Correct mistakes at once. Do not scribble so hard that the word cannot be read. Draw one neat line through a wrong word and write the correction beside it, if your teacher allows that.

### Family information on a form
Some forms ask for a parent, a guardian or the number of brothers and sisters. Write what is true in your family. A guardian is a person who looks after a child. Families are not all the same, and the form only needs the facts it asks for.

## Key words
• instructions — the directions that tell you how to fill a form
• print — writing in which each letter stands separately and is easy to read
• guardian — a person who looks after a child

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The instruction says "Write the date as day/month/year". The learner writes 2017 March 14. What should be written instead, using the sample date?

Working:
1. Day comes first: 14.
2. Month comes next: March, or 03 if numbers are required.
3. Year comes last: 2017.
4. The instruction in this example uses day/month/year.

Answer: 14/03/2017 or 14 March 2017, matching the way the form asks for the month.

### Example 2
A learner leaves "Name of head teacher" empty because she is not sure. Is that better than inventing a name?

Working:
1. A form should be true.
2. An invented name would mislead the reader.
3. She should ask the teacher, then fill the blank.

Answer: Yes. She should ask and then fill the true name, not invent one.

## Activity: Fill a class form together
You will need: A printed form with personal details and school details, Pens, The list of instructions on the form
1. Read the instructions aloud together before you write.
2. Fill your own name, grade and date of birth. Use school details your teacher confirms.
3. Record any family detail the form asks for, such as the name of a parent or guardian.
4. Swap with a partner and check labels, capital letters, the date and empty blanks.
5. Correct neatly and keep the form clean enough to display.

## Practice
1. What should you do first when you receive a form?
2. Rewrite this name in the way a capital-letter instruction requires: peter kamau.
3. The sample date of birth is 14 March 2017. Write it as day/month/year using numbers.
4. A form says "Name of parent or guardian". What do you write?

## Summary
• Read the instructions before you fill any blank.
• Put each true fact on the line that asks for it, in clear print.
• Check capital letters, the date order and empty blanks with a partner.

### Answers to practice
1. Read the title and the instructions before writing.
2. PETER KAMAU
3. 14/03/2017
4. The true name of your parent or of the guardian who looks after you.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Why careful forms matter

LESSON 3: WHY CAREFUL FORMS MATTER
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what goes wrong when a form is incomplete or untrue.
• Fill a form neatly enough for someone else to read.
• Create a simple form and tell why each blank is there.

Curriculum outcomes: b) fill information in forms correctly for self- expression; c) realise the importance of filling forms correctly for effective communication

## Introduction
Suppose a library had three cards for one learner, and the name was spelled a different way on each card. The librarian would not know which card to trust. Careful writing on a form prevents that kind of mix-up.

## Notes
### What careful filling does
A form is a message. The person who reads it may never meet you. They know only what you wrote.

- A clear name means the right person gets the club place, the book or the certificate.
- A correct grade puts you in the right group.
- A correct date of birth shows your age for a race, a visit or a health card.
- A correct school address lets a letter find the school.

If a blank is skipped, the reader has to guess or send the form back. If a word is unreadable, the reader may copy it wrongly. If a detail is untrue, the record is unfair to other people and can cause trouble later. Filling a form is a job for honesty as well as for neatness.

### Display and peer review
When the class displays forms, readers should be able to stand a short distance away and still read the names. That is a good test of print.

Let a partner review your form. Thank them for pointing out a missing capital letter or a cramped word. Do not laugh at another learner's handwriting. Help them rewrite the hard line. Love in a classroom looks like patience with someone who is still learning.

### Creating your own form
You can make a form for a real class need, such as a reading-club list or a family-visitor record for a class play. A useful form has:

1. A title that states the purpose.
2. One short instruction, such as "Write in print" or "Use capital letters for names".
3. Only the blanks you truly need. For a reading club: Name, Grade, Title of book, Date borrowed.
4. Enough space to write.

Do not ask for private facts you do not need. A reading-club form does not need a date of birth.

Type the form on a computer, laptop or tablet if your teacher provides one, or write it neatly on paper. If you download a form from the internet, do it with your teacher. Do not type personal details into a website unless the teacher and a parent have agreed.

### A last look
Before a form leaves your hands, read it as if you were the stranger who must use it. Every label should have a true, tidy answer. That habit makes communication work.

## Key words
• record — information kept so it can be used later
• review — to look at work carefully and suggest improvements
• purpose — the reason something is made or done

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A reading-club form asks for the learner's date of birth, home address and favourite food, but the club only needs to know who borrowed which book. Which blanks are unnecessary?

Working:
1. The club needs the borrower and the book.
2. Date of birth, home address and favourite food are not needed for that purpose.
3. Extra private details should be left off a form you create.

Answer: Date of birth, home address and favourite food are unnecessary for a simple borrowing list.

### Example 2
Why is an unreadable name a problem even if it is spelled correctly?

Working:
1. The reader cannot be sure of the letters.
2. The wrong person may be recorded.
3. A form must communicate without a second explanation.

Answer: The reader may copy the wrong person, so the message fails.

## Activity: Create and display a form
You will need: Paper or a computer, laptop or tablet, Pens or a keyboard, A wall or table for display
1. In pairs, choose a purpose linked to family or school, such as a reading club or a class visitor list.
2. Write a title, one instruction and four useful labels with blanks.
3. Type the form if a device is available, or write it in neat print. If you use the internet, follow your teacher's guidance and do not enter private details.
4. Fill one copy with sample or real class details your teacher approves.
5. Display the forms, review a partner's form kindly, and say why each blank is needed.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for filling a form correctly.
2. Name two things a good form that you create should have.
3. Why should a reading-club form not ask for a home address if the club does not need it?
4. What does it mean to review a partner's form with respect?

## Summary
• A form is a message to someone who may never meet you, so it must be true and clear.
• Create forms that ask only for the facts they need.
• Review a partner's form kindly and display work you are proud to show.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: so the right person is recorded; so letters and certificates reach the right place; so the reader does not have to guess; so the record is true.
2. A title that shows the purpose, and clear labels with enough space. An instruction such as "Write in print" also belongs on it.
3. Private information should be collected only when it is needed.
4. Point out missing or unclear details kindly, and help them correct the work without laughing at them.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 1.4.1 WRITING: FUNCTIONAL WRITING
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which set is personal details?
   A. School name, address, head teacher
   B. Name, grade, date of birth
   C. Book title, date borrowed, librarian
   D. Class teacher, school name, grade

2. Which label asks for a school detail?
   A. Date of birth
   B. Name of head teacher
   C. Learner's first name
   D. Gender

3. What should you read before you write on a form?
   A. Only the first blank
   B. The instructions
   C. Another learner's answers
   D. The back of the page only

4. The instruction says "Use capital letters for names". Which entry follows it?
   A. amina yusuf
   B. Amina yusuf
   C. AMINA YUSUF
   D. amina Yusuf

5. Write the sample date 14 March 2017 as day/month/year in numbers.

6. A learner writes the class teacher's name on the line "Name of head teacher". What is the mistake?

7. Why is it a problem to invent a school address?
   A. Addresses are always secret
   B. The record would be untrue and a letter might not arrive
   C. Forms must be written in pencil
   D. The date of birth would change

8. Why should a form you create ask only for needed facts?

9. Which instruction belongs on a neat class form?
   A. Leave the name blank
   B. Write in print
   C. Guess any date
   D. Use a different fact for each label

10. What is the main reason to fill forms carefully?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 1.4.1 WRITING: FUNCTIONAL WRITING
========================================

1. B. Name, grade, date of birth
   Name, grade and date of birth are facts about the learner.

2. B. Name of head teacher
   The head teacher is part of the school details.

3. B. The instructions
   Instructions tell you how the information must be written.

4. C. AMINA YUSUF
   Every letter in the name is a capital letter.

5. 14/03/2017
   The day is 14, the month March is 03, and the year is 2017.

6. The fact does not match the label. The head teacher's name belongs on that line.
   Each blank collects one particular fact.

7. B. The record would be untrue and a letter might not arrive
   A form must carry true information so that it can be used.

8. So that private details are not collected without a reason, and the form stays easy to fill.
   A reading list does not need a date of birth.

9. B. Write in print
   Print keeps the form easy to read.

10. So the reader gets the right information and can act on it without guessing.
   A form is a message. Unclear or untrue details break that message.

2. Think of the true fact that matches it.
3. Write neatly in print, on the line, not above the label.
4. Start names with capital letters: Amina Yusuf, not amina yusuf.
5. Write Grade as a number if that is what the form shows, for example 4.
6. Write the date of birth in the order the instruction gives.

In class you may fill a practice form with your own school details. If you are not sure of the school's address or the head teacher's name, leave that blank empty until the teacher tells you. An empty blank you still need to check is better than a made-up address.

### A worked form
Instructions: Write in print. Use capital letters for names. Write the date as day, month, year.

Name: AMINA YUSUF
Grade: 4
Date of birth: 14 March 2017
School: GREEN VALLEY PRIMARY SCHOOL
Address: P.O. BOX 25, HILL ROAD
Class teacher: MR OTIENO
Head teacher: MRS WANJALA

This is still the sample pupil from the previous lesson. Notice that every instruction was kept: print, capital letters for names, and the date in day-month-year order.

### Check with a partner
Swap forms. Ask these questions:

- Is every required blank filled?
- Is each fact next to the right label?
- Are names easy to read?
- Does the date follow the instruction?
- Would a stranger understand it without asking?

Correct mistakes at once. Do not scribble so hard that the word cannot be read. Draw one neat line through a wrong word and write the correction beside it, if your teacher allows that.

### Family information on a form
Some forms ask for a parent, a guardian or the number of brothers and sisters. Write what is true in your family. A guardian is a person who looks after a child. Families are not all the same, and the form only needs the facts it asks for.

## Key words
• instructions — the directions that tell you how to fill a form
• print — writing in which each letter stands separately and is easy to read
• guardian — a person who looks after a child

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The instruction says "Write the date as day/month/year". The learner writes 2017 March 14. What should be written instead, using the sample date?

Working:
1. Day comes first: 14.
2. Month comes next: March, or 03 if numbers are required.
3. Year comes last: 2017.
4. The instruction in this example uses day/month/year.

Answer: 14/03/2017 or 14 March 2017, matching the way the form asks for the month.

### Example 2
A learner leaves "Name of head teacher" empty because she is not sure. Is that better than inventing a name?

Working:
1. A form should be true.
2. An invented name would mislead the reader.
3. She should ask the teacher, then fill the blank.

Answer: Yes. She should ask and then fill the true name, not invent one.

## Activity: Fill a class form together
You will need: A printed form with personal details and school details, Pens, The list of instructions on the form
1. Read the instructions aloud together before you write.
2. Fill your own name, grade and date of birth. Use school details your teacher confirms.
3. Record any family detail the form asks for, such as the name of a parent or guardian.
4. Swap with a partner and check labels, capital letters, the date and empty blanks.
5. Correct neatly and keep the form clean enough to display.

## Practice
1. What should you do first when you receive a form?
2. Rewrite this name in the way a capital-letter instruction requires: peter kamau.
3. The sample date of birth is 14 March 2017. Write it as day/month/year using numbers.
4. A form says "Name of parent or guardian". What do you write?

## Summary
• Read the instructions before you fill any blank.
• Put each true fact on the line that asks for it, in clear print.
• Check capital letters, the date order and empty blanks with a partner.

### Answers to practice
1. Read the title and the instructions before writing.
2. PETER KAMAU
3. 14/03/2017
4. The true name of your parent or of the guardian who looks after you.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why careful forms matter
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: WHY CAREFUL FORMS MATTER
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what goes wrong when a form is incomplete or untrue.
• Fill a form neatly enough for someone else to read.
• Create a simple form and tell why each blank is there.

Curriculum outcomes: b) fill information in forms correctly for self- expression; c) realise the importance of filling forms correctly for effective communication

## Introduction
Suppose a library had three cards for one learner, and the name was spelled a different way on each card. The librarian would not know which card to trust. Careful writing on a form prevents that kind of mix-up.

## Notes
### What careful filling does
A form is a message. The person who reads it may never meet you. They know only what you wrote.

- A clear name means the right person gets the club place, the book or the certificate.
- A correct grade puts you in the right group.
- A correct date of birth shows your age for a race, a visit or a health card.
- A correct school address lets a letter find the school.

If a blank is skipped, the reader has to guess or send the form back. If a word is unreadable, the reader may copy it wrongly. If a detail is untrue, the record is unfair to other people and can cause trouble later. Filling a form is a job for honesty as well as for neatness.

### Display and peer review
When the class displays forms, readers should be able to stand a short distance away and still read the names. That is a good test of print.

Let a partner review your form. Thank them for pointing out a missing capital letter or a cramped word. Do not laugh at another learner's handwriting. Help them rewrite the hard line. Love in a classroom looks like patience with someone who is still learning.

### Creating your own form
You can make a form for a real class need, such as a reading-club list or a family-visitor record for a class play. A useful form has:

1. A title that states the purpose.
2. One short instruction, such as "Write in print" or "Use capital letters for names".
3. Only the blanks you truly need. For a reading club: Name, Grade, Title of book, Date borrowed.
4. Enough space to write.

Do not ask for private facts you do not need. A reading-club form does not need a date of birth.

Type the form on a computer, laptop or tablet if your teacher provides one, or write it neatly on paper. If you download a form from the internet, do it with your teacher. Do not type personal details into a website unless the teacher and a parent have agreed.

### A last look
Before a form leaves your hands, read it as if you were the stranger who must use it. Every label should have a true, tidy answer. That habit makes communication work.

## Key words
• record — information kept so it can be used later
• review — to look at work carefully and suggest improvements
• purpose — the reason something is made or done

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A reading-club form asks for the learner's date of birth, home address and favourite food, but the club only needs to know who borrowed which book. Which blanks are unnecessary?

Working:
1. The club needs the borrower and the book.
2. Date of birth, home address and favourite food are not needed for that purpose.
3. Extra private details should be left off a form you create.

Answer: Date of birth, home address and favourite food are unnecessary for a simple borrowing list.

### Example 2
Why is an unreadable name a problem even if it is spelled correctly?

Working:
1. The reader cannot be sure of the letters.
2. The wrong person may be recorded.
3. A form must communicate without a second explanation.

Answer: The reader may copy the wrong person, so the message fails.

## Activity: Create and display a form
You will need: Paper or a computer, laptop or tablet, Pens or a keyboard, A wall or table for display
1. In pairs, choose a purpose linked to family or school, such as a reading club or a class visitor list.
2. Write a title, one instruction and four useful labels with blanks.
3. Type the form if a device is available, or write it in neat print. If you use the internet, follow your teacher's guidance and do not enter private details.
4. Fill one copy with sample or real class details your teacher approves.
5. Display the forms, review a partner's form kindly, and say why each blank is needed.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for filling a form correctly.
2. Name two things a good form that you create should have.
3. Why should a reading-club form not ask for a home address if the club does not need it?
4. What does it mean to review a partner's form with respect?

## Summary
• A form is a message to someone who may never meet you, so it must be true and clear.
• Create forms that ask only for the facts they need.
• Review a partner's form kindly and display work you are proud to show.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: so the right person is recorded; so letters and certificates reach the right place; so the reader does not have to guess; so the record is true.
2. A title that shows the purpose, and clear labels with enough space. An instruction such as "Write in print" also belongs on it.
3. Private information should be collected only when it is needed.
4. Point out missing or unclear details kindly, and help them correct the work without laughing at them.

questions.question: Which set is personal details?
questions.explanation: Name, grade and date of birth are facts about the learner.

questions.question: Which label asks for a school detail?
questions.explanation: The head teacher is part of the school details.

questions.question: What should you read before you write on a form?
options: The back of the page only
questions.explanation: Instructions tell you how the information must be written.

questions.question: The instruction says "Use capital letters for names". Which entry follows it?
questions.explanation: Every letter in the name is a capital letter.

questions.question: Write the sample date 14 March 2017 as day/month/year in numbers.
questions.explanation: The day is 14, the month March is 03, and the year is 2017.

questions.question: A learner writes the class teacher's name on the line "Name of head teacher". What is the mistake?
questions.answer: The fact does not match the label. The head teacher's name belongs on that line.
questions.explanation: Each blank collects one particular fact.

questions.question: Why is it a problem to invent a school address?
options: The record would be untrue and a letter might not arrive
Forms must be written in pencil
The date of birth would change
questions.explanation: A form must carry true information so that it can be used.

questions.question: Why should a form you create ask only for needed facts?
questions.answer: So that private details are not collected without a reason, and the form stays easy to fill.
questions.explanation: A reading list does not need a date of birth.

questions.question: Which instruction belongs on a neat class form?
options: Use a different fact for each label
questions.explanation: Print keeps the form easy to read.

questions.question: What is the main reason to fill forms carefully?
questions.answer: So the reader gets the right information and can act on it without guessing.
questions.explanation: A form is a message. Unclear or untrue details break that message.
